shots.name: q1-lexington
shots.what: Q1: clicking the Lexington and Concord diamond in the bookmark view (pop-up shown on the feature)
shots.popup:
The Battle of Lexington and Concord 

April 19, 1775 

The Battle of Lexington and Concord was the first battle of the American Revolution. Leading up to this conflict, there was unrest in the Massachusetts colony caused by restrictive British policies and taxes. The British governor of the Mas​s​achusetts colony, Governor Gage, inflamed tensions by harshly enforcing British law. He drafted the Coercive Acts, which punished colonists for deeds of defiance against the king, such as the Boston Tea Party. Colonists who fought against British rule in favor of independence became known as Patriots.
By April 1775, Governor Gage was facing the threat of outright rebellion. He hoped to prevent violence by seizing weapons and gunpowder being stored in Concord, Massachusetts, 20 miles northwest of Boston.
But Patriot spies learned of Gage's plan. On the evening of April 18, Paul Revere and others raised the alarm that British soldiers were on their way to Concord. Minute Men and militias rushed to confront them early on April 19. As the British soldiers passed through Lexington on their way to Concord, they came face to face with the Patriot militia. When the British soldiers started across the village green, the militia retreated. In the confusion, a shot was fired. Though no one knows who fired the first shot that day, it effectively began the war.
From Lexington, the British soldiers continued toward Concord. There, they met more Patriot militia members. Alarmed by the number of militia members gathered, the British retreated toward Boston. Along the way, they were ambushed by Patriot militia members. 

Image credit: Courtesy the National Guard Bureau

shots.name: q2-bunkerhill
shots.what: Q2: clicking a diamond (Bunker Hill) at the zoomed-out view
shots.popup:
The Battle of Bunker Hill 

June 17, 1775 

The Patriots were defeated at the Battle of Bunker Hill, but they proved they could hold their own against the British Army. The battle was a tactical victory for the British, but it was a sobering experience. The British sustained twice as many casualties as the Patriots and lost many officers. The fierce fight confirmed that any reconciliation between England and the American colonies was no longer possible.

British commander in chief General Sir Thomas Gage was under pressure from his superiors to quash the colonial rebellion. The British army planned to launch an attack against the Patriots on the heights north and south of Boston. Details of the attack were leaked, and a detachment of 1,000 Massachusetts and Connecticut soldiers gathered to defend a hill in Charlestown. The violent clash of these forces signaled that the colonial revolt would not be easily extinguished. 

Image credit: John Trumbull

Battle Details

Fall of New York City

1776 

After forcing Washington's army to retreat from Long Island in the Battle of Brooklyn, the British build on their advantage. They continued attacking American forces across New York. Moving north across Manhattan, they defeated the Americans at Fort Washington and captured 3,000 soldiers. The British take control of New York City. They maintained that stronghold for the remainder of the war. 

Victor: Britain

shots.name: q2-oregon
shots.what: Q2: clicking the Oregon Trail (west of where the trails split)
shots.popup:
Pony Express Trail

The Pony Express was a mail service that could deliver mail from St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento, California in 10 days. With a system of 153 stations each located 16-24 kilometers (10-15 miles) apart so that riders could stop for fresh horses, mail could travel more than 2897 kilometers (1,800 miles) in just 10 days. At the time, mail was typically carried by stagecoach on the Butterfield Overland Trail, which could take several weeks. It could also be taken by trail to the Isthmus of Panama, where it was transferred to a ship headed north to California. While not as fast as today’s mail, the Pony Express played an important role in connecting the West to Eastern cities.

The Pony Express trail, also known as the Overland Route, followed the Mormon Pioneer trail through Salt Lake City, then headed straight across Nevada to the mountain pass the Donner Party used to reach California. The service only operated for 18 months between April 1860 and October 1861, when a transcontinental telegraph line was completed.

Virginia in 1790

1790 census: 747,610 people, 292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%).

Counted for the House under the three-fifths clause: 630,559. That gave Virginia 19 House seats in 1793 (one for every 33,000 people), plus 2 senators, like every state.

If enslaved people had been counted in full: 22 seats. If they had not been counted at all: 13 seats.

Virginia's census figure excludes Kentucky, which was counted separately. Today's state outlines, with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia, as they were in the 1790s.

shots.name: q4-mcculloch
shots.what: Q4: the pop-up for the McCulloch v. Maryland square
shots.popup:
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)

Question: Could Congress charter a national bank, and could a state tax it?

Ruling: Congress could charter the bank, and Maryland's tax on it was unconstitutional and void.

Why it matters: Congress may use appropriate means to carry out its powers, and federal law is supreme over state law: "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."

Why here: Maryland sued James McCulloch, a cashier at the Baltimore branch of the Bank of the United States, to collect a state tax on the bank.

Source

shots.name: q2-neworleans
shots.what: Q2: clicking one of the biggest diamonds (New Orleans)
shots.popup:
New Orleans

January 8, 1815 

American Side Victory 

Total Casualties: 2,096 
____________________________________________________

The United States achieved its greatest land victory of the War of 1812 at New Orleans. The battle ended a British effort to gain control of a critical American port and elevated Maj. Gen. Andrew Jackson to national fame. The British launched a forward attack against American forces at Chalmette Plantation. British casualties far outnumbered those of the Americans. Jackson's fame from the battle contributed to him winning the presidential election thirteen years later.

The British strategy had been to focus on attacking American coastal regions to cripple American trade and transportation. Although they had been unable to take Baltimore, the British moved ahead with a plan to attack New Orleans.

The Americans were aware of a possible invasion on the Gulf Coast. Andrew Jackson reached the city on December 1 and began assembling an army. His force consisted of Tennessee and Kentucky frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, New Orleans businessmen, free men of color, Choctaw warriors, smuggler Jean Lafitte and his privateers, sailors, marines, and United States troops.

On January 8, 1815, Maj. Gen. Andrew Jackson's hastily assembled army won the day against a battle-hardened and numerically superior British force. The resounding American victory at the Battle of New Orleans soon became a symbol of American democracy triumphing over the old European ideas of aristocracy and entitlement. The battle was the last major armed engagement between the United States and Britain.
